o: From each index, the jump you make is completely determined: an odd jump goes to the smallest index j > i with arr[j] >= arr[i], and an even jump goes to the smallest index j > i with arr[j] <= arr[i]. So the process is deterministic — each index has at most one odd-successor and one even-successor. A naive simulation from every start is O(n^2) worst case (e.g. a strictly increasing array makes every jump land on the next index, but adversarial inputs can force long chains). The key observation is that we only care whether the *end* is reachable, so we can work backwards with DP over states (index, parity of next jump). In Example 1, index 3 jumps odd to 4 (the end), so 3 is good; index 4 is trivially good; indices 0–2 dead-end after one or two jumps. In Example 2, following the forced chains shows only starts 1, 3, 4 reach index 4.
k: The jump destination from any index is unique per parity, so the whole process is a deterministic walk — no branching to explore.
Define odd[i] = can reach the end if the *next* jump from i is odd; even[i] similarly. Then odd[i] = even[oddNext(i)] and even[i] = odd[evenNext(i)], computed right-to-left.
The 'smallest j > i with arr[j] >= arr[i]' (and its mirror for <=) can be precomputed for all i in O(n log n) via a sorted traversal plus a monotonic stack.

a.i: For each starting index, simulate the deterministic jump process until we either reach the last index or get stuck. Each jump requires scanning forward for the best candidate, costing O(n), and a chain can be O(n) long, giving O(n^2) overall. This is fine conceptually and passes small inputs but TLEs on large adversarial cases like strictly decreasing arrays where odd jumps repeatedly scan far ahead.
s: For each start index s, set cur = s, parity = odd.
Scan j from cur+1 to n-1 tracking the best candidate per the current parity rule (value tie broken by smaller index).
If no candidate exists, this start fails; if cur == n-1 at any point, count it.
Flip parity and repeat until stuck or end reached.
Return the count of good starts.
a.t: O(n^2) — each of n starts may scan up to n candidates per jump along an O(n)-long chain.
a.sp: O(1) extra space beyond the input.

a.n: Approach 2: Monotonic Stack Precomputation + Backward DP (Optimal)
a.i: Precompute, for every i, oddNext[i] (smallest j>i with arr[j]>=arr[i]) and evenNext[i] (smallest j>i with arr[j]<=arr[i]). Process indices in order of value (ties by index): when inserting index i into a stack of already-inserted (smaller-valued) indices, any popped index k had i as the nearest greater-or-equal element to its right — exactly oddNext[k]. Doing the same pass in decreasing value order yields evenNext. Then DP backwards: odd[i] = even[oddNext[i]] (or true if oddNext is the last index), even[i] = odd[evenNext[i]]. Answer = number of i with odd[i] true, since every journey starts with an odd jump.
s: Sort indices by (value, index). Sweep in that order maintaining a monotonic decreasing stack of indices; when pushing index i, pop k's and set oddNext[k] = i.
Repeat the same sweep sorted by (-value, index) to fill evenNext[k] = i (nearest smaller-or-equal to the right).
Initialize odd[n-1] = even[n-1] = true; all other entries false.
Iterate i from n-2 down to 0: if oddNext[i] exists, odd[i] = even[oddNext[i]]; if evenNext[i] exists, even[i] = odd[evenNext[i]].
Count indices with odd[i] true and return the count.
a.t: O(n log n) — two sorts dominate; the stack sweeps and DP are O(n).
a.sp: O(n) — successor arrays, DP arrays, and stack.

w: In an interview, lead with the brute force to show you understand the deterministic-jump structure, then pivot to the optimal solution: precompute successors with a value-ordered monotonic stack and run a two-state backward DP. Common pitfalls: forgetting that ties in value must resolve to the *smallest index* (handle it in the sort key); confusing which DP state feeds which (odd[i] depends on even[oddNext[i]], since parities alternate); and off-by-one issues at the last index (both states are true there, and it counts as one good start). Edge cases: single-element array returns 1; arrays with many duplicates stress the tie-breaking. Follow-ups might ask to reconstruct an actual good path (store parent pointers during DP) or to handle streaming updates (an ordered set / TreeMap gives the same complexity without sorting).
